title: Chapter 11 — Liberty Of The Press In The United States
paragraphs: The influence of the liberty of the press does not affect political opinions alone; it extends to all of men's opinions and modifies customs as well as laws. In another part of this work I shall try to determine the degree of influence that the liberty of the press has exercised on civil society in the United States, and to indicate the direction it has given to the ideas, as well as the tone it has imparted to the character and feelings, of the Anglo-Americans. For now, I propose simply to examine the effects produced by the liberty of the press in the political world.

I confess that I do not feel toward the liberty of the press the firm and complete attachment that things supremely good in their very nature tend to excite in the mind. I approve of it more from a recollection of the evils it prevents than from consideration of the advantages it ensures.

If anyone could point out an intermediate yet tenable position between the complete independence and the entire subjection of public opinion, I should perhaps be inclined to adopt it. But the difficulty is to find that position. If your intention is to correct the abuses of an unlicensed press and to restore the use of orderly language, you may at first try the offender before a jury; but if the jury acquits him, the opinion that was that of a single individual becomes the opinion of the country at large. Too much and too little has therefore been done. If you press on, you must bring the offender before a court of permanent judges. But even here the case must be heard before it can be decided; and the very principles no book would have ventured to avow are now blazoned forth in the pleadings. What was obscurely hinted at in a single composition is then repeated in a multitude of other publications. The language in which a thought is expressed is the mere carcass of the thought, not the idea itself; tribunals may condemn the form, but the sense and spirit of the work are too subtle for their authority. Too much has still been done to retreat, too little to reach your end; so you must press on. If you establish a censorship of the press, the public speaker's tongue will still make itself heard, and you have only increased the mischief. The powers of thought do not depend, like those of physical strength, on the number of their mechanical agents, nor can a host of authors be counted like the troops that compose an army. On the contrary, the authority of a principle is often increased by the smallness of the number of men who express it. The words of a strong-minded man, penetrating the passions of a listening assembly, have more power than the shouts of a thousand orators; and if free speech is allowed in any one public place, the consequence is the same as if it were allowed in every village. The liberty of discourse must therefore be destroyed as well as the liberty of the press; this is the necessary end of your efforts. But if your object was to repress the abuses of liberty, they have brought you to the feet of a despot. You have been led from the extreme of independence to the extreme of subjection without meeting a single tenable position for shelter or repose.

Certain nations have special reasons for cherishing the liberty of the press, apart from the general motives I have just pointed out. For in certain countries that profess to enjoy the privileges of freedom, every individual agent of the Government may violate the laws with impunity, since those whom he oppresses cannot prosecute him before the courts of justice. In this case the liberty of the press is not merely a guarantee, but the only guarantee, of the liberty and security the citizens possess. If the rulers of these nations propose to abolish the independence of the press, the people would be justified in saying: give us the right to prosecute your offenses before the ordinary tribunals, and perhaps we may then waive our right of appeal to the tribunal of public opinion.

But in countries where the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people ostensibly prevails, the censorship of the press is not only dangerous but absurd. When the right of every citizen to take part in the government of society is acknowledged, every citizen must be presumed capable of distinguishing between the different opinions of his contemporaries, and of weighing the different facts from which inferences may be drawn. The sovereignty of the people and the liberty of the press may therefore be regarded as correlative institutions, just as the censorship of the press and universal suffrage are two things irreconcilably opposed, which cannot long be kept together among the institutions of the same people. Not a single individual of the twelve millions who inhabit the territory of the United States has yet dared to propose any restriction on the liberty of the press. The first newspaper I laid eyes on upon my arrival in America contained the following article:

In all this affair the language of Jackson has been that of a heartless despot, concerned only with the preservation of his own authority. Ambition is his crime, and it will be his punishment too: intrigue is his native element, and intrigue will confound his tricks and deprive him of his power. He governs by means of corruption, and his immoral practices will redound to his shame and confusion. His conduct in the political arena has been that of a shameless and lawless gamester. He succeeded at the time, but the hour of reckoning approaches, and he will be forced to disgorge his winnings, throw aside his false dice, and end his days in some retirement where he may curse his madness at leisure—for repentance is a virtue his heart is likely never to know.

In France it is not uncommonly imagined that the virulence of the press comes from the uncertain social condition, the political excitement, and the general sense of consequent evil that prevail in that country; and it is therefore supposed that once society regains a certain degree of composure, the press will give up its present vehemence. I am inclined to think that these causes explain the extraordinary ascendancy it has gained over the nation, but that they have little influence on the tone of its language. The periodical press seems to me to be driven by passions and tendencies independent of the circumstances in which it is placed, and the present condition of America bears this out.

America is perhaps at this moment the country in the whole world that contains the fewest germs of revolution; yet the press is no less destructive in its principles than in France, and it shows the same violence without the same grounds for indignation. In America, as in France, it constitutes a singular power, so strangely composed of mingled good and evil that it is at once indispensable to the existence of freedom and nearly incompatible with the maintenance of public order. Its power is certainly much greater in France than in the United States, though nothing is rarer in the latter country than to hear of a prosecution having been brought against it. The reason is perfectly simple: the Americans, having once admitted the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people, apply it with perfect consistency. It was never their intention to found a permanent state of things with elements that undergo daily modification; and so there is nothing criminal in attacking the existing laws, provided the attack is not accompanied by a violent breach of them. They are of the opinion, moreover, that courts of justice are unable to check the abuses of the press, and that since the subtlety of human language perpetually eludes the severity of judicial analysis, offenses of this kind tend to escape the hand that tries to seize them. They hold that to act effectively on the press it would be necessary to find a tribunal not only devoted to the existing order of things, but capable of surmounting the influence of public opinion—a tribunal that would conduct its proceedings without publicity, pronounce its decrees without stating its reasons, and punish the intentions even more than the language of an author. Whoever had the power of creating and maintaining such a tribunal would waste his time in prosecuting the liberty of the press, for he would be the supreme master of the whole community, and he would be as free to rid himself of the authors as of their writings. On this question, then, there is no middle ground between servitude and extreme license; to enjoy the priceless benefits the liberty of the press ensures, one must submit to the inevitable evils it engenders. To expect to gain the former and escape the latter is to cherish one of those illusions that commonly mislead nations in their times of sickness—when, tired with faction and exhausted by effort, they try to combine hostile opinions and opposing principles on the same soil.
The small influence of the American journals is attributable to several reasons, among them the following:

The liberty of writing, like every other liberty, is most formidable when it is a novelty; for a people that has never been accustomed to take part in the conduct of State affairs places implicit confidence in the first tribune who arouses its attention. The Anglo-Americans have enjoyed this liberty ever since the founding of the settlements; besides, the press cannot of its own power create human passions, however skillfully it may kindle them where they exist. In America politics are discussed with animation and a varied activity, but they rarely touch those deep passions that are stirred whenever the positive interest of a part of the community is damaged. And in the United States the interests of the community are in a most prosperous condition. A single glance at a French and an American newspaper is enough to show the difference between the two nations on this point. In France the space given to commercial advertisements is very limited, and the news items are not extensive; the most essential part of the journal is that which contains the discussion of the politics of the day. In America three-quarters of the enormous sheet set before the reader are filled with advertisements, and the rest is frequently occupied by political news or trivial anecdotes; only from time to time does one find a corner devoted to passionate discussions like those with which the journalists of France are accustomed to indulge their readers.

Observation has shown, and the innate shrewdness of the pettiest as well as the greatest of despots has discovered, that the influence of a power is increased in proportion as its direction is made more central. In France the press combines a twofold centralization: almost all its power is concentrated in the same spot and vested in the same hands, for its organs are far from numerous. The influence of a public press so constituted upon a skeptical nation must be unbounded. It is an enemy with which a Government may sign an occasional truce, but which it is difficult to resist for any length of time.

Neither kind of centralization exists in America. The United States has no metropolis; the intelligence as well as the power of the country are dispersed abroad, and instead of radiating from a single point, they cross each other in every direction. The Americans have established no central control over the expression of opinion, any more than over the conduct of business. These are circumstances that do not depend on human foresight; but it is owing to the laws of the Union that there are no licenses to be granted to printers, no securities demanded from editors as in France, and no stamp duty as in France and formerly in England. As a result, nothing is easier than to set up a newspaper, and a small number of readers is enough to cover the editor's expenses.

The number of periodical and occasional publications that appear in the United States actually surpasses belief. The most enlightened Americans attribute the subordinate influence of the press to this excessive dissemination; and it is adopted as an axiom of political science in that country that the only way to neutralize the effect of public journals is to multiply them indefinitely. I cannot conceive why a truth so self-evident has not already been more generally admitted in Europe. It is understandable that those who hope to bring about revolutions by means of the press should want to confine its action to a few powerful organs; but it is perfectly incredible that the partisans of the existing state of things, and the natural supporters of the law, should try to diminish the influence of the press by concentrating its authority. The Governments of Europe seem to treat the press with the courtesy of the knights of old; they are eager to furnish it with that same central power they have found to be so trusty a weapon, so as to enhance the glory of their resistance to its attacks.

In America there is scarcely a hamlet that does not have its own newspaper. It is easy to imagine that neither discipline nor unity of design can be imposed on so scattered a host, and each one is consequently led to fight under his own standard. All the political journals of the United States are indeed arrayed on the side of the administration or against it; but they attack and defend in a thousand different ways. They cannot succeed in forming those great currents of opinion that overwhelm the most solid obstacles. This division of the influence of the press produces a variety of other consequences scarcely less remarkable. The ease with which journals can be established draws a multitude of individuals into them; but since the extent of competition rules out the possibility of considerable profit, the most distinguished classes of society are rarely led to take up these undertakings. Yet such is the number of public prints that, even if they were a source of wealth, writers of ability could not be found to direct them all. The journalists of the United States are usually placed in a very humble position, with scanty education and a vulgar turn of mind. The will of the majority is the most general of laws, and it establishes certain habits that become the marks of each particular class of society; thus it dictates the etiquette practiced at courts and the etiquette of the bar. The characteristic of the French journalist consists in a violent, but frequently eloquent and lofty, manner of discussing the politics of the day; the exceptions to this habitual practice are only occasional. The characteristic of the American journalist consists in an open and coarse appeal to the passions of the populace; he habitually abandons the principles of political science to assail the characters of individuals, to pursue them into private life, and to disclose all their weaknesses and errors.

Nothing can be more deplorable than this abuse of the powers of thought. I shall have occasion later to point out the influence of the newspapers on the taste and the morality of the American people, but my present subject concerns only the political world. It cannot be denied that the effects of this extreme license of the press tend indirectly to the maintenance of public order. Individuals who already stand high in the esteem of their fellow citizens are afraid to write in the newspapers, and are thus deprived of the most powerful instrument they could use to excite the passions of the multitude to their own advantage. *a

a [ They only write in the papers when they choose to address the people in their own name; as, for instance, when they are called upon to repel calumnious imputations, and to correct a misstatement of facts.]

The personal opinions of the editors carry no weight whatever in the eyes of the public. The only use of a journal is that it conveys the knowledge of certain facts, and it is only by altering or distorting those facts that a journalist can contribute to the support of his own views.

But although the press is limited to these resources, its influence in America is immense. It is the power that drives the circulation of political life through all the districts of that vast territory. Its eye is constantly open to detect the secret springs of political designs and to summon the leaders of all parties to the bar of public opinion. It rallies the interests of the community around certain principles and draws up the creed that factions adopt; for it provides a means of communication between parties that hear one another and address one another without ever being in direct contact. When a great number of the organs of the press adopt the same line of conduct, their influence becomes irresistible; and public opinion, when perpetually assailed from the same side, eventually yields to the attack. In the United States each individual journal exercises but little authority, but the power of the periodical press is second only to that of the people. *b
b [ See Appendix, P.]
The opinions established in the United States under the empire of the liberty of the press are often more firmly rooted than those formed elsewhere under the sanction of a censor.

In the United States democracy perpetually raises fresh individuals to the conduct of public affairs, and so the measures of the administration are seldom regulated by strict rules of consistency or of order. But the general principles of the Government are more stable, and the opinions most prevalent in society are generally more durable than in many other countries. Once the Americans have taken up an idea, whether well or ill founded, nothing is harder than to root it out of their minds. The same tenacity of opinion has been observed in England, where, for the last century, greater freedom of conscience and more invincible prejudices have existed than in all the other countries of Europe. I attribute this to a cause that may at first sight seem to have an opposite tendency: to the liberty of the press. Nations among which this liberty exists are apt to cling to their opinions out of pride as much as out of conviction. They cherish them because they hold them to be just, and because they exercised their own free will in choosing them; they maintain them not only because they are true, but because they are their own. Several other reasons lead to the same end.

A man of genius once remarked that "ignorance lies at the two ends of knowledge." It would perhaps have been more accurate to say that absolute convictions are to be found at the two extremes, and that doubt lies in the middle. For the human intellect may be considered in three distinct states, which frequently succeed one another. A man believes implicitly, because he adopts a proposition without inquiry. He doubts as soon as he is assailed by the objections his inquiries may have aroused. But he often succeeds in satisfying these doubts, and then he begins to believe afresh: he no longer grasps a truth in its most shadowy and uncertain form, but sees it clearly before him, and advances by the light it gives him. *c
c [ It may, however, be doubted whether this rational and self-guiding conviction arouses as much fervor or enthusiastic devotedness in men as their first dogmatical belief.]

When the liberty of the press acts upon men who are in the first of these three states, it does not immediately disturb their habit of believing implicitly, without investigation; but it constantly modifies the objects of their intuitive convictions. The human mind continues to make out only one point in the whole intellectual horizon, and that point is in continual motion. Such are the symptoms of sudden revolutions, and of the misfortunes sure to befall those generations which abruptly adopt the unconditional freedom of the press.

The circle of novel ideas, however, is soon exhausted; the touch of experience is upon them, and the doubt and mistrust their uncertainty produces become universal. We may be sure that the majority of mankind will either believe without knowing why, or will not know what to believe. Few are the beings who can ever hope to reach that state of rational and independent conviction which true knowledge can beget in defiance of the attacks of doubt.

It has been remarked that in times of great religious fervor, men sometimes change their religious opinions, whereas in times of general skepticism everyone clings to his own persuasion. The same thing happens in politics under the liberty of the press. In countries where all the theories of social science have in turn been contested, the citizens who have adopted one of them stick to it, not so much because they are convinced of its excellence, as because they are not convinced of the superiority of any other. In the present age, men are not very ready to die in defense of their opinions, but they are rarely inclined to change them; and there are fewer martyrs as well as fewer apostates.

Another, still more compelling reason may be added: when no abstract opinions are regarded as certain, men cling to the mere inclinations and external interests of their position, which are naturally more tangible and more permanent than any opinions in the world.

It is no easy question whether aristocracy or democracy is more fit to govern a country. But it is certain that democracy annoys one part of the community, and that aristocracy oppresses another part. When the question is reduced to the simple expression of the struggle between poverty and wealth, the tendency of each side of the dispute becomes perfectly clear without further debate.
